title: I KNOW WHAT I WANT TO SELL. NOW WHAT?
content:
You do not need a complete business plan before you can say you know what you want to sell.

You need a direction specific enough that your unanswered questions are now about this business rather than every business you could possibly start.

DRAFT FINAL CHECK
Can you answer these questions?
1. What am I selling?
2. Who is it for?
3. Why does this direction fit me or appeal to me?
4. What causes me to make money when the customer buys?
5. If repeat purchases or payments matter, what specifically causes me to get paid again?
6. What do I still need to investigate, verify, create, source, or test?

DRAFT BUSINESS DIRECTION STATEMENT
I want to sell [specific product, service, or access] to [specific customer] because [specific problem or value]. I expect to make money through [one-off purchase, replenishment/reorders, recurring subscription, service fee, commission, etc.]. Before I commit, I still need to verify [important unknowns].

EXAMPLES
I want to create a one-off digital guide for first-time dog owners who want a practical plan for their puppy's first month.

I want to explore an own-brand protein powder produced by a contract manufacturer for women who struggle to consume enough protein.

I want to offer monthly remote bookkeeping to small home-service businesses.

I want to explore software that customers pay monthly to access because it solves a recurring workflow problem.

DRAFT CLOSING
If you can write your own version of that statement, you have solved the problem this library was built to help you solve.

You have something to sell.

The next question is:
HOW WILL YOU SELL IT?

That is the job of the separate HOW DO I SELL IT? system.

SPECIFIC ENOUGH TO MOVE FORWARD
Compare "I want to sell products online," "I want to sell supplements," and "I want to explore an own-brand protein powder produced by a contract manufacturer for women who struggle to consume enough protein." The last statement still has unanswered questions, but they are now useful questions about a specific direction.

KEEP YOUR VERIFICATION LIST
Supplier quotes, regulations, licenses, testing, compensation plans, market demand, current program terms, and other external facts may still need research. That does not mean you failed to finish this library.

WHAT YOU HAVE ACCOMPLISHED
You began with "How can I make money online?" You can now replace it with something closer to: "This is what I want to sell, this is who it is for, this is how the sale would create income, and these are the things I still need to verify."

That is enough to move to the next problem without dragging every other business model with you.

FINAL SELF-CHECK
A useful finished direction should survive these questions:
Can another person understand what I mean by the thing I sell?
Can I name the customer without saying "everyone"?
Can I explain what creates the payment?
If I expect repeat income, can I explain what creates the next payment too?
Can I separate what I know from what I still need to verify?
Do I know which questions now belong to research and which belong to the future HOW DO I SELL IT? system?

If yes, stop browsing business models. You have a direction to work on.

ONE LAST DISTINCTION
A business direction is not a business promise. You are allowed to discover during research that the supplier is too expensive, the regulations change the idea, customers do not want it, the workload is unrealistic, or another version makes more sense.

That does not send you back to "I have no idea what to sell." It gives you evidence you can use to revise a direction that is already much more specific.

YOUR FINAL ANSWER CAN BE PROVISIONAL
A strong ending might be:

"I want to investigate providing monthly remote bookkeeping for small home-service businesses. I would earn through a recurring service fee. I still need to verify the exact scope I can offer, required credentials or insurance, realistic capacity, and pricing."

That is specific enough to move forward while remaining honest about what is not known yet.

WHAT A FINISHED DIRECTION SHOULD TELL YOU

By this point, your answer should be specific enough that a stranger could understand the basic business without hearing a list of every model you considered.

Compare:

"I want to sell digital products."

with:

"I want to create a one-off digital guide for first-time dog owners that helps them prepare for the first month at home."

Or:

"I want to sell health products."

with:

"I want to investigate creating my own branded protein powder through a contract manufacturer for women who struggle to consume enough protein."

Or:

"I want to freelance."

with:

"I want to offer recurring remote bookkeeping for small home-service businesses."

The second version in each pair is not a finished business plan. It is simply specific enough to create useful next questions.

YOUR BUSINESS DIRECTION STATEMENT

Write one paragraph that answers:

What am I considering selling?

Who is it for?

What problem, need, desire, or job does it address?

What kind of purchase is it: one-off, consumable, subscription, service, or a deliberate combination?

Do I own the product or service, or am I participating in the sale of someone else's?

How does the first payment happen?

If I expect repeat income, what specifically creates the next payment?

Why does this direction fit my skills, interests, resources, or preferences?

What still needs to be verified before I treat the idea as viable?

WHAT COMES AFTER THIS LIBRARY

The next stage is not to reopen every business model and keep comparing forever. It is to investigate the direction you chose.

That may mean validating customer demand, checking suppliers, reviewing licenses or program terms, understanding regulations, testing costs, defining an offer, or building the first version.

After you know what you are actually selling, a different question becomes useful:

How will the right customer find it, understand it, trust it, and buy it?

That is the job of HOW DO I SELL IT?

You do not need the whole business solved before leaving this library. You need a direction clear enough that your uncertainty has become specific. That is progress you can work with.

IF YOU ARRIVE HERE WITH TWO POSSIBLE DIRECTIONS

Do not force certainty just to finish the worksheet.

Write both directions in the same format and identify the unresolved question separating them.

For example:

DIRECTION A: I want to sell my own branded consumable through a contract manufacturer.

DIRECTION B: I want to begin by recommending an existing consumable through a program that retains customer attribution.

UNRESOLVED QUESTION: Am I willing and financially able to take on product development, minimum orders, and product ownership now, or do I want to begin with another company's product?

That is still progress.

Use the unresolved question to decide what to investigate next. Once it is answered, update the direction statement.

The endpoint is clarity, not pretending you have no uncertainty.

THE ENDPOINT

You are finished with this library when you can state what you intend to sell, who it is for, how the purchase creates revenue for you, and which important uncertainties still need investigation. That is a business direction, not proof that the business will succeed.

WHERE TO GO NEXT
Do not keep reopening branches because you feel as though you should know more. If you can state what you want to sell, who it is for, how the transaction creates income, and what remains to be verified, this library has done its job.

The unresolved question is now HOW DO I SELL IT? That is intentionally outside this product.

OPTIONAL NEXT STEP: WANT HANDS-ON HELP FROM HERE?

You can absolutely take what you have learned here and build your business on your own. But if you would rather have people helping you as you build, there is another option.

I currently build through Amway while developing one-off information products like this one and exploring subscription products as another part of my business. I am taking a somewhat different approach to network marketing than the coaches I work with, and I want to be transparent about that.

My coaches have experience building through a more traditional network-marketing model. I am charting a newer path by combining that foundation with information products and other ways of generating income. If you decide to work with us, I would encourage you to learn from their experience as your foundation, then experiment with my approach too if it fits what you want to build.

THE COACHING ITSELF IS FREE, BUT IT IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY AVAILABLE TO EVERYONE.

We use an interview process before deciding to work with someone. There is a practical reason for that: if you build a successful business with us, your success can contribute to ours too. That gives us a reason to invest real time in helping you succeed rather than charging you by the hour for coaching.

But free does not mean our time has no value. Coaching works best when someone is interested in learning, following through, and actually building. The interview process gives us a chance to get to know each other, answer questions, and decide whether working together makes sense before either side commits their time.

AND NETWORK MARKETING IS NOT THE ONLY WAY I PLAN TO LET PEOPLE BUILD ALONGSIDE ME.

My goal is to make some of my information products available through options such as Master Resell Rights and/or affiliate programs. That could allow someone to build around products I create without joining Amway at all.

So if you want hands-on coaching and you are interested in exploring the network-marketing side, you can apply to talk with us.

If you like what I am building but network marketing is not for you, you can explore the information-product opportunities as they become available.

And if neither interests you, take the business direction you found in this library and go build it your way.

You do not need to choose my business. The whole point was to help you choose yours.
